title: Gradient microstructure and nanohardness in the plastic boundary layer of an AA5083 aluminum alloy processed by local high-pressure torsion
abstract: Abstract Local High-Pressure Torsion (L-HPT) is a recently developed technological process that induces severe plastic deformation (SPD) within a boundary layer (BL) beneath a slowly rotating punch pressed against a metallic plate. In contrast to conventional high-pressure torsion (HPT), where the severe plastic deformation zone extends through the entire thickness of the processed metallic disk, the depth of such a zone and its microstructure after L-HPT are not known in advance and have not been previously investigated. Such novel results, obtained using scanning electron microscopy and nanoindentation, are presented in this work for an AA5083 aluminum alloy as a model system. Unlike conventional dry friction conditions, where BL thickness typically does not exceed ~ 10 μm, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) measurements have revealed that the BL with an ultrafine-grained (UFG) structure that develops near the contact interface between an AA5083 aluminum alloy sample and a rotating punch can reach the thickness of up to 500 μm, starting from about 2 mm distance from the rotation center. A gradient microstructure is observed in this region, with an average grain size of about 100–200 nm in the layer immediately adjacent to the punch surface with a thickness of about 50 μm. Within this layer, a Mackenzie-type random misorientation distribution is identified, associated with extreme shear strain and saturation flow stress. This is accompanied by a slightly noticeable trend toward an increase in nanohardness in the vicinity of the contact surface. The discussion of the experimental results encompasses analytical description and finite element simulation.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The high-pressure torsion (HPT) process, aimed at intense refinement of the microstructure and significant improvement in mechanical properties of metals and alloys, can be traced back to [ 1 ] and belongs to the most well-known methods of imposing severe plastic deformation (SPD) [ 2 ]. Numerous studies have demonstrated the efficiency of HPT in producing ultrafine-grained structures and the evolution of strain homogeneity across the disk thickness [ 3 ]. Surface friction between the processed disk-type sample and mutually rotating anvils under high pressure enforces the disk to deform by shear. The severe plastic deformation zone extends through the entire thickness of the processed metallic disk. Different versions of HPT have been proposed, e.g., that for high-pressure tube twisting [ 4 ].

Local High-Pressure Torsion (L-HPT) is a newly developed technological process where a punch pressed with simultaneous rotation penetrates deeply into a metallic plate [ 5 ]. It can be viewed as a combination of HTP (compression with a rotating anvil) and typical punching (indentation of a non-rotating punch into a thick plate). In distinction to the well-known friction stir processing (FSP), e.g., [ 6 ,  7 ] the angular velocity of punch rotation in the L-HPT process is orders of magnitude lower, which makes the process essentially isothermal due to heat sinking in the surrounding material. Typically, rotation speed is only a few revolutions per minute, and the temperature in the sample rises by no more than 50 °C under a contact pressure of the order of 1 GPa. While a repeatable L-HPT process can lead in applications to desired heterogeneous patterns of hardened areas on a plate surface, the present study is focused on the material microstructure and nanohardness distributions beneath a single rotating punch. In contrast to conventional high-pressure torsion (HPT), the severe plastic deformation zone in L-HTP cannot extend through the entire thickness of the indented plate and must be limited to a narrower zone beneath the rotating punch, which is called a boundary layer (BL). Thickness of that BL and microstructure within it after L-HPT have not been previously investigated. The aim of the present work is to provide such novel results, obtained using scanning electron microscopy and nanoindentation, for an AA5083 aluminum alloy treated as a model system.

Analogous thin surface layers in metals, also called BLs and featuring gradient submicrocrystalline structures, are of considerable interest for the development of heterostructured materials—an emerging frontier in materials science [ 8 ,  9 ]. Recent perspectives emphasize the importance of gradient and heterogeneous microstructures formed under SPD conditions for advanced mechanical performance [ 10 ]. For this reason, processes such as burnishing [ 11 ,  12 ], deep cold rolling [ 13 ], hammer peening [ 14 ], and plastic flow machining [ 15 ] are actively being explored as platforms for studying BL formation and evolution. Nevertheless, plastic BLs in solids—arising under friction and plastic deformation—remain comparatively underexplored. This gap is consistent with broader observations that localized deformation zones and heterogeneous microstructures produced by SPD are still insufficiently characterized [ 16 ]. Only a limited number of studies have addressed their theoretical and experimental observation.

The classical work by Oldroyd [ 17 ] laid the foundation for the theory of plastic boundary layers in Bingham-type materials. In that paper, using the equations of two-dimensional flow of a Bingham solid, the existence of a thin layer of intense shear adjacent to a rigid boundary was demonstrated for the first time. Oldroyd’s work [ 17 ] introduced the very notion of a  plastic boundary layer . Building on this foundation, subsequent models of plastic BLs were developed. In [ 18 ,  19 ], Oldroyd’s theory was extended to a broader class of BL-formation problems in various pipes and channels. The authors [ 18 ,  19 ] showed that, when the wall shear stress is sufficiently high, a plastic layer emerges whose thickness increases along the flow direction, while a “rigid plug” is preserved outside the layer. These solutions directly employ the structure of Oldroyd’s equations and his idea of separating the flow domain into a plastic BL and an elastic-rigid region. The study [ 20 ] further develops Oldroyd’s approach for a more general class of viscoplastic materials. The author emphasizes that the BL structure persists even for complex rheological models, with Oldroyd’s classical solution representing a special case.

In [ 21 ], a BL model was developed for the first time within the framework of classical plasticity theory, without assuming viscoplasticity. In paper [ 22 ], an alternative approach to describing boundary layers was proposed—the  Third Body  concept—in which the thin interfacial zone of intense shear is treated as a distinct material with its own yield surface, internal variables, and structural evolution. That approach naturally encompasses processes occurring in tribological contacts and during cold welding.

In [ 23 ], high-speed in situ visualization combined with particle image velocimetry (PIV) analysis revealed the formation of a thin near-surface plastic BL along a rigid indenter. This layer is interpreted as a Bingham-like plastic boundary layer in which friction-induced flow is localized, whereas the adjacent bulk deforms predominantly as a rigid body. The study [ 24 ], using in situ visualization, demonstrated the nucleation and development of a shear band in metals during cutting. The authors interpret the shear band as a BL arising in a zone of intense shear between two rigid regions. In [ 25 ], combining experiment and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, the nucleation and evolution of a BL under contact friction were demonstrated. Thus, in works [ 23 ,  24 – 25 ], plastic BLs are experimentally investigated either at the interface between an elastic material and a rigid wall or within a nearly rigid body.

One of the few examples of systematic investigation of a plastic BL is presented in [ 26 ], where a gradient layer up to 250 μm thick is formed on a copper surface as a result of a tribological test. Unlike the experimental studies discussed above, [ 26 ] examines a boundary layer that forms between a rigid tool surface and the adjacent bulk plastic flow. The authors performed detailed microstructural mapping along the surface normal, identified zones with different levels of accumulated strain, and analyzed EBSD maps and nanohardness. They showed that the BL is a complex multilayered structure formed by intense shear and subsequent competition between grain refinement, dynamic recrystallization, and substructural hardening. However, even such a detailed study leaves open key questions regarding the mechanics of plastic flow within the BL, the nature of the transition from the tribo-zone to bulk deformation, and the way in which localized flow interacts with the ultrafine-grained structure. These issues require further study.

In the present work, we investigate samples of the AA5083-H116 aluminum alloy processed by the L-HPT method. In contrast to the tribological tests in [ 26 ], where the gradient structure forms due to the higher-speed sliding (60 rpm), local heating, and mechanical mixing, the L-HPT process implements a fundamentally different deformation regime. At a low rotation speed (5 rpm) and a pressure of about 1 GPa, a plastic boundary layer is formed quasi-isothermally, governed by deep shear deformation beneath the punch rather than by surface friction. Using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) techniques, particularly electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), we examine the ultrafine-grained structure in the deformed zones near the punch. Mechanical properties of the material in this region are determined by nanoindentation. The experimental analysis is supplemented by finite element modeling and simplified analytical description of the strain distribution within the BL.

sections.heading: Materials and methodology of L-HPT
paragraphs: Figure  1  shows a schematic diagram of the L-HPT process. It shows a punch 1, which is pressed with simultaneous rotation into the plate 2. The angular velocity of punch rotation in the L-HPT process is 2–3 orders of magnitude lower than in friction stir processing (FSP), e.g., [ 6 ] which makes these processes fundamentally different due to the dominant influence of dynamic and thermal factors in FSP. Prior to L-HPT processing, the surface of the aluminum plate was degreased using 96% ethanol to ensure clean contact conditions. During the experiment, the punch was impressed into the plate at a translational speed of 0.1 mm/s and an angular velocity of five revolutions per minute. The total processing time was 40 s. The punch had a diameter of 10 mm, and the average contact pressure applied during the process was approximately 1GPa. Figure 1 Schematic diagram of L-HPT: 1-punch, 2-metal plate.

To assess thermal effects, a thermocouple was embedded in the plate at a distance of 10 mm from the punch edge. Temperature measurements showed that during the entire L-HPT process, the temperature increase did not exceed 50 °C, confirming the quasi-isothermal nature of deformation under the selected conditions. A detailed description of the L-HPT experimental procedure is provided in [ 5 ].

The plates for the study were made of AA5083 aluminum alloy having the nominal chemical composition as follows (in wt.%): Mg 4,81%; Mn 0,53%; Fe 0,32%; Cu 0,07%; Si 0,09%; Cr 0,10%; Zn 0,02%; Ti 0,01%; Al balance. The mean grain size of the material in the initial state was equal to 17 μm. A specimen for microstructural characterization and nanohardness measurements was extracted from the workpiece after L-HPT processing, and the RD–ND cross section through the center of the punch impression was analyzed. Standard metallographic specimen preparation, up to polishing with a 1-μm particle-sized diamond suspension, was performed using a Struers Rotopol-11 grinding/polishing machine. The next step, aimed at achieving a deformation-free surface for EBSD characterization, was vibratory polishing using QATM’s Qpol Vibro vibratory polisher—initially with a 0.25 μm monocrystalline diamond Gel2 + , followed by final polishing with 0.04 μm colloidal silica.

sections.heading: Methodology of EBSD and nanohardness measurements
paragraphs: EBSD measurements were performed on a Zeiss CrossBeam 350 SEM equipped with a Hikari Super EBSD detector. Orientation maps were obtained using an accelerating voltage of 10 kV and a 120 μm aperture. Maps were acquired at various magnifications to enable analysis at different levels of detail. Initially, three maps at lower magnification with a step size of 2 μm were acquired and merged to provide an overview of the boundary layer formed by L-HPT processing. Subsequently, strip areas measuring 20 μm × 225 μm were analyzed from the edge (punch contact zone) toward the bulk using a scanning step size of 60 nm to study microstructural changes—namely, grain refinement and variation in misorientation angle—as a function of distance from the edge. The reported analysis was conducted at four selected locations along the punch-sample contact zone. Additionally, a smaller strip (5 μm × 60 μm), located within one of the analyzed regions, was examined in greater detail using a 20-nm scanning step to determine grain size in the near-surface zone with higher resolution. Data analysis was performed using OIM Analysis™ 8 and ATEX software [ 27 ].

Nanoindentation tests were carried out on the material in strip 3 of BL and the reference material to demonstrate the relationship between microstructure changes and an increase in hardness. The Anton Paar (previously CSM, Switzerland) Ultra-Nano-Hardness Tester (UNHT) with a Berkovich tip was used. The tip was calibrated on a fused silica sample. The tests were conducted in a load control mode, in the quasi-static regime (loading time 30 s, unloading time 30 s and 2 s hold time). The hardness was calculated on the basis of load-penetration depth curves using the Oliver–Pharr method. For the deformed material, in strip 3, more than 240 indentation spaced 5 μm apart were made. The maximum applied load was 1 mN, corresponding to a penetration depth of approximately 130 nm. Strip 3 was divided into 12 fragments, each 20 µm long and containing 20 indents. The hardness corresponding to each fragment was calculated as the mean of the values determined in each of the 20 tests. The hardness of the reference material was determined at two loads: 1 mN and 40 mN. At a load of 1 mN, the hardness was calculated as the mean of 69 tests spaced 5 µm apart. At a load of 40 mN, the hardness was calculated as the mean of 12 tests spaced 120 µm apart.

sections.heading: Methodology of FEM
paragraphs: The calculations were performed using the commercial software package QForm-3D (version QForm UK 10.3.1) [ 28 ]. The three-dimensional (3D) geometric model of the L-HPT was identical to the diagram shown in Fig.  1 . The blank was initially automatically divided into a mesh consisting of 13,227 four-node tetrahedral finite elements. In the event of significant deformations causing severe distortion of the elements, the mesh was automatically rebuilt. As a result, the final mesh contained up to 67,885 elements. It should be noted that no systematic study of the grid’s sensitivity has been conducted; therefore, the results of the FEM should be interpreted primarily in qualitative terms.

sections.heading: Experimental results
paragraphs: Figure  2  presents an EBSD map of half of the axial section of the sample in the contact zone with the punch. Despite the limited spatial resolution, which does not allow individual grains in the finest structured region to be fully resolved, a zone of distinctive grain refinement is clearly observed near the surface, extending to a depth of approximately 200–500 μm. This zone, characterized by a progressive decrease in resolvable grain morphology and an increase in local orientation scatter as the grain size approaches from above the applied EBSD step size (~ 2 μm), is identified as the boundary layer (BL). While the EBSD step size does influence the apparent sharpness of the transition, which can be more diffuse in reality, the BL is not an artifact of spatial resolution. The subsequent results confirm the existence of a near-surface region of pronounced gradient of grain refinement, of an approximate thickness of ~ 200–500 μm, through quantitative analysis of grain size, misorientation distributions, texture evolution and nanohardness. Figure 2 EBSD visualization of the specimen axial section adjacent to the punch. The trace of BL, in the form of an UFG layer, is noticeable.

The specified layer (BL) is naturally associated with high local deformation in the area of contact between the material and the punch. Figure  3  shows enlarged images of four characteristic strip areas adjacent to the punch, allowing for a more detailed characterization of the microstructure. It can be seen that in strip 1, located along the axis of symmetry, a relatively coarse-grained structure is preserved and BL is absent. The EBSD map in strip 1 does not differ from that for the reference material; therefore, the latter is omitted. With increasing distance from the axis (strips 2, 3, and 4), progressive development of BL into the depth of the material is observed, due to increasing accumulated plastic deformation along the radius beneath the rotating punch. Figure 3 EBSD maps of representative areas of the axial section of the sample in the contact zone with the punch. The diagram at the top of the figure shows the location of these areas.

Figure  4  shows the evolution of the microstructure of the material as the distance from the contact surface with the punch increases, using strip 3 as an example. The strip 3 is a narrow strip of dimensions 20 μm × 225 μm, along which five square cells 10 μm × 10 μm were evenly distributed (see Fig.  4 ). The first cell is located directly at the boundary with the punch, while the others are equidistant from each other in the direction of the material depth. The corresponding microstructures, misorientation-angle distribution diagrams and local pole figures are shown for them. Figure 4 Evolution of the microstructure of the material in strip 3 (see Fig.  2 ) as the distance from the contact surface with the punch increases. On the right-hand side of the enlarged microstructures within square cells, diagrams of the misorientation angle distribution over the corresponding cell and local pole figures are shown.

In the immediate vicinity of the contact zone (first cell), the distribution corresponds to the Mackenzie curve [ 32 ], which is typical for a quasi-stationary submicroscopic structure formed at advanced stages of severe plastic deformation [ 33 ]. For cells located at a greater distance from the punch surface, two distinct distribution peaks are observed—at small and large dislocation angles. At the same time, as the depth into the sample volume increases, the intensity of the first peak increases, while that of the second decreases. The first peak indicates the continuing fragmentation of the original grains, while the second reflects the change in orientation of the already fragmented grains [ 34 ].

The pole figures reveal a progressive evolution of crystallographic texture with increasing distance from the contact surface. In the region closest to the punch (5 μm), the diffuse intensity indicates a weak texture with a nearly random orientation distribution associated with the ultrafine microstructure. At intermediate depths (55–105 μm), localized intensity maxima emerge, indicating the development of preferred orientations. Further from the surface (155–205 μm), the pole figures exhibit sharper and more intense peaks, reflecting the formation of a well-defined texture with typical ⟨111⟩ and ⟨100⟩ fiber components. This gradual transition from a weak, diffuse texture near the surface to a stronger, well-defined texture at greater depths correlates with increasing mean grain size and a shift in misorientation-angle distributions toward lower angles.

For a quantitative analysis of the evolution of the grain structure depending on the distance to the punch surface, the entire strip 3 was divided along its length into ten equal fragments. For each of them, the average grain sizes and corresponding standard deviations were determined. The assessment was based on an EBSD map obtained with a scanning step of 60 nm. The obtained values are presented in Fig.  5  as a graph of the dependence of the average grain size on the distance to the contact zone with the punch. The obtained dependence indicates the formation of a gradient structure. As the distance to the punch decreases, both the average grain size and the corresponding standard deviation decrease, which indicates an increase in the degree of microstructure uniformity in the zone of intense deformation. At the same time, in the immediate vicinity of the contact surface (within a few tens of micrometers), there is a tendency for the curve to flatten, which may indicate the achievement of a quasi-stationary state of the structure in the boundary zone. Figure 5 Diagram showing the dependence of the average grain size on the distance to the contact zone with the punch. Evaluation based on an EBSD map obtained with a scanning step of 60 nm (blue) and 20 nm (red). See detailed explanation in the text.

For a more detailed analysis of the subsurface zone (0–60 µm from the contact surface), an EBSD map was obtained with a scanning step of 20 nm. This area was divided along its length into fragments of approximately 10 µm, for each of which the average grain size was also determined. The corresponding part of the graph in Fig.  5  is highlighted in red. A detailed analysis shows that in the immediate vicinity of the contact zone boundary, the average grain size changes insignificantly, which indicates the establishment of a quasi-stationary structure. This conclusion is consistent with the previously noted random nature of the distribution of misorientation angles in this area.

This conclusion is also consistent with the almost stationary dependence of the measured nanohardness of the material in strip 3 on the distance to the boundary with the punch, shown in Fig.  6 . Despite fairly pronounced fluctuations in values, there is only slightly noticeable trend toward an increase in nanohardness in the vicinity of the contact surface. According to [ 33 ], when a quasi-stationary microstructure is formed, the hardness is expected to reach saturation, which is compatible with the trend observed in Fig.  6 . However, it should be noted that the nanohardness measurements might be affected by the surface preparation process. Figure 6 Dependence of the nanohardness in BL on the distance to the boundary with the punch, in comparison with the hardness of the reference material.

Furthermore, the nanoindentation size effect is known to increase nanohardness with decreasing indentation load. This effect is attributed to the increase in the plastic strain gradient in vicinity of the sharp indenter tip at small loads, which induces the growth of density of the so-called geometrically necessary dislocations that cause additional hardening of the material [ 36 ].

The mean hardness values of the reference material at loads of 1 mN and 40 mN are 1980 MPa and 1410 MPa, respectively, and are shown in Fig.  6  with marked standard deviation. The hardness of the reference material at a load of 1 mN is thus considerably higher than that at a load of 40 mN. Since the 1 mN test itself induces an increase in the measured hardness, it does not adequately reflect the increase in hardness caused by the SPD process. A more adequate estimation of this increase can be obtained by comparing the results of the indentation tests at a 40 mN load, namely, the mean hardness of ~ 2200 MPa measured in the deformed strip equivalent by symmetry to strip 3, and 1410 MPa in the reference material. Note that the discrepancy between the mean hardness values at loads of 1 mN and 40 mN is less pronounced in the deformed BL than in the reference material. For loads greater than 500 mN, corresponding to the microscale and unaffected by size effect, the Vickers hardness of the reference material, as measured with a Berkovich tip, is HV IT  = 110, which is close to the HV value reported in [ 5 ].

sections.heading: Discussion of experimental results
paragraphs: The structural features observed in the L-HPT process differ markedly from those reported for conventional high-pressure torsion (HPT) and friction stir processing (FSP) of Al–Mg alloys. Unlike conventional HPT, which typically generates through-thickness uniform ultrafine-grained (UFG) structures [ 2 ], L-HPT induces localized plastic flow with pronounced strain gradient in both the normal and tangential directions to the punch surface, resulting in a BL of variable thickness and microstructural heterogeneity. Compared to FSP, which operates at elevated temperatures and promotes dynamic recrystallization [ 6 ], the quasi-isothermal conditions of L-HPT favor grain fragmentation and the formation of non-equilibrium high-angle boundaries.

In the present study, the BL formed during L-HPT exhibits a gradient structure with grain sizes ranging from ~ 100 nm near the punch surface to ~ 2 μm at greater depths of 200 μm (see Fig.  5 ). In contrast, FSP of similar Al–Mg alloys typically results in grain sizes of 0.5–2 μm depending on the location relative to the tool path and thermal exposure [ 6 ]. Moreover, the nature of high-angle boundaries differs significantly: in FSP, they arise primarily through continuous dynamic recrystallization and are stabilized by thermal effects and second-phase particles, while in L-HPT, boundaries are formed under extreme shear deformations at relatively low temperatures.

These distinctions highlight the unique deformation pathway and structural outcome of L-HPT, offering complementary insights into boundary layer formation under severe plastic deformation. The presented results allow us to draw an important qualitative conclusion. In the near-surface region, a misorientation distribution close to the Mackenzie distribution is observed, indicating a high degree of randomization of the crystallographic structure and, correspondingly, a weakening of the texture in this zone. This finding is consistent with the concept of achieving a quasi-steady state under large deformations, at which texture evolution slows significantly.

Furthermore, there is data in the literature showing that during Severe Plastic Deformation processes with pronounced flow localization (in particular, during plastic flow machining [ 15 ]), near-surface layers with sharply defined gradients of deformation, structure, and texture are formed (see, for example, [ 35 ]). This indicates that in our case, the boundary layer is characterized not only by a gradient of grain size and deformation, but also by a texture gradient.

Beyond the fundamental differences in deformation mechanisms, L‑HPT also offers important engineering advantages. As demonstrated in [ 5 ], localized severe deformation enables the formation of regular patterns of hardened zones—ring‑shaped structures, meshes, and discrete strengthened patches. Such architected configurations are fully consistent with the modern concepts of heterostructured materials [ 8 ,  9 ], where the interaction between zones with contrasting mechanical properties leads to superior strength–ductility combinations and enhanced functional performance. The gradient microstructure and near‑surface stabilization observed in the present study indicate that L‑HPT may serve as an effective tool for producing surfaces with tailored stiffness gradients, improved resistance to crack propagation, and enhanced tribological behavior. These promising effects warrant further experimental verification under different L‑HPT processing conditions.

It is noteworthy that the observed grain sizes in the near-surface zone (~ 100–200 nm) and hardness stabilization are in good agreement with known data on the saturation of the Al–Mg alloy structure during HPT. In particular, for A5086 it was shown that under large deformations the grain stabilizes at a level of about 250–300 nm, and the hardness reaches a plateau [ 37 ]. A review of contemporary HPT data also indicates that Al–Mg alloys are characterized by reaching a steady state at grain sizes of 100–300 nm [ 38 ]. Thus, the formation of a quasi-steady-state structure in BL is consistent with the general saturation mechanism characteristic of Al–Mg systems under severe plastic deformation.

It is known that during dry friction of metals, due to localized shear deformation, a thin layer of material with UFG structure is formed on the contact surface [ 25 ]. Its thickness, as a rule, does not exceed the value close to 10 μm. According to Fig.  2 , the thickness of BL in the L-HPT process is significantly greater and reaches a value of about 200–500 μm in the transition zone adjacent to the punch surface. We attribute the significant increase in BL thickness to the fact that during L-HPT, the material surrounding BL undergoes plastic deformation, unlike under friction conditions, where the material remains in an elastic state within the volume of the contacting bodies. An argument in favor of this hypothesis is the qualitative coincidence of the BL geometry with the location of the zone of increased plastic deformation and its gradients, as shown in Fig.  7 . Figure 7 Distribution of effective strain at L-HPT of AA5083 H116 alloy. The calculation is performed using the finite element method in the QForm package. The calculation conditions are specified in Sect. " Methodology of FEM ".

To clarify the physical nature of the boundary layer identified above, the following interpretation can be proposed. In the present study, the boundary layer (BL) is defined not by a single threshold parameter, but by a change in the deformation regime, analogous to classical concepts of the boundary layer in fluid mechanics. In this sense, the BL is interpreted as a near-surface region where the material’s response differs fundamentally from that in the bulk.

The bulk material is characterized by hardening during deformation, accompanied by a significant increase in the yield stress, as described in the literature for the corresponding deformation processes [ 5 ]. In contrast, the near-surface region examined in this study exhibits a quasi-steady state, as evidenced by the stabilization of hardness (and, accordingly, yield stress) and the formation of an ultrafine-grained microstructure with a characteristic grain size that is significantly smaller than that in the bulk. Furthermore, a pronounced gradient of grain refinement is observed in BL, as the grain size changes 20x (from 100 nm to 2 μm) over the distance 200 μm across BL (Fig.  5 ), and much slower (8.5 × from 2 μm to 17 μm over the distance of several mm) in the bulk material outside BL.

Within the BL, two physically distinct regions can be identified. The quasi-stationary region corresponds to the near-surface zone, where saturation is reached, the yield stress changes only slightly, and the grain size approaches a steady-state value. Beneath it lies the accommodation zone, which is a transition zone characterized by strong strain gradients and microstructural features. In particular, this region exhibits a pronounced grain size gradient, reflecting the transition from the coarse-grained main region to the ultrafine-grained quasi-stationary region, while strain hardening is already significantly reduced. As a result, further grain refinement within this regime produces only a minor increase in hardness, in agreement with the universal behavior reported for SPD-processed Al–Mg alloys. Thus, the plastic boundary layer can be regarded as a transition region from the hardening bulk region to the saturation state near the surface. It is characterized not only by high levels of plastic deformation but also by strong strain gradients and a sharp change in structural features, primarily grain size.

In the next section, based on some fairly natural assumptions, we will discuss the dependence of effective deformation on the distance to the punch boundary, assumed flat, as well as to the rotation axis.

sections.heading: Analysis of shear strain distribution in BL
paragraphs: The magnitude of externally imposed circumferential displacement during L-HPT varies proportionally to the punch radius. The deformation beneath the rotating punch can be modeled as simple shear in the circumferential direction on the plane orthogonal to the rotation axis, with other strain components being less significant. Consequently, the subsequent discussion focus on the simple shear deformation that varies proportionally with the distance from the rotation axis, which is possible in a perfectly plastic layer. However, the possible slip of the material on the punch surface, if varying nonlinearly along the radius, can induce additional shearing on a cylindrical surface in the material beneath the punch. According to the Levy–Mises constitutive equations, this can restore consistency with a slight hardening trend, as visible in Fig.  6 . The respective analysis is omitted here due to the lack of comparable experimental data. The numerical values of plastic shear strain and effective strain within BL are estimated below at a radius of ~ 2 mm or greater, corresponding to the microstructure visualized in Fig.  4 .

It is postulated that the assumptions adopted are acceptable for describing the region of large strain adjacent to the punch at L-HPT. First, at large strains, the material hardening under saturation conditions can be neglected, and the material can be considered perfectly plastic. Secondly, dry friction is realized at the contact with the punch, the stress of which can be considered as limiting. Finally, in a sufficiently thin layer of the material, in close proximity to the punch, a state of simple shear occurs. As one moves away from the surface, the stress–strain state of the material becomes more complex.

It should be emphasized that the self-similarity assumption used in this section is locally asymptotic. Strictly speaking, this assumption applies not to the entire BL, but rather to its quasi-stationary region, where the microstructure and flow stress of the material are virtually constant. However, the change in flow stress becomes small throughout the BL, as revealed by the nanohardness measurements. In such circumstances, the strain field acquires local asymptotic self-similarity, which justifies the use of expression ( 14 ) as a first approximation for describing the shape of the strain distribution within the BL.

Equation ( 15 ) provides a compact analytical description of the strain gradient within the boundary layer (BL). Its exponential form reflects the steep spatial variation of plastic deformation near the punch, which is consistent with experimental observations. This relation is particularly useful for modeling microstructural evolution and mechanical response in the BL region, where high strain gradients govern grain refinement, texture development, and hardness distribution. By parameterizing the effective strain as a function of distance, Eq. ( 15 ) enables integration of experimental data into numerical simulations and facilitates predictive analysis of deformation-induced phenomena.

It is important to emphasize, however, that in the present paper, the exponential dependence is not introduced as a result of empirical data fitting, but follows from the assumption of self-similarity of the deformation field in the near-surface region. The main purpose of Eq. ( 15 ) is to define a functional form of the deformation distribution that reflects its rapid increase as it approaches the surface, characteristic of problems with pronounced deformation localization (similar to the behavior of fields in boundary layers). The use of two characteristic points serves only to estimate the order of magnitude of the parameters γ 0  and  l  and does not claim to define them precisely. In this sense, the parameters should be regarded as effective characteristics that define the scale of deformation change.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The present study has revealed previously unknown characteristics of the boundary layer (BL), adjacent to the rotating punch surface, formed in an AA5083 H116 aluminum alloy during the Local High-Pressure Torsion (L-HPT). The BL exhibits a submicron crystalline gradient structure and reaches a thickness of approximately 200–500 µm, depending on the radial position. Notably, this is at least an order of magnitude greater than the typical BL thickness observed on elastically deformable substrates under dry friction conditions, highlighting the profound influence of substrate plasticity on the BL development observed here.

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis performed with different scanning steps revealed a pronounced gradient of average grain size within the BL, ranging from ~ 100 nm near the contact surface to ~ 2 µm at a depth of ~ 200 µm. In the near-surface zone (~ 50 µm), grain size variation is small, with the average grain size ranging from 100 to 200 nm. The microstructure in this zone exhibits features of a quasi-stationary state, with a random misorientation angle distribution of Mackenzie type. A slightly noticeable trend toward an increase in nanohardness in the vicinity of the contact surface is consistent with saturation of the flow stress. These characteristics are also consistent with the accumulation of extreme shear strains, typical of severe plastic deformation.

The BL can be regarded as a mechanical and structural transitory zone between frictional stresses at the contact surface and plastic flow in the bulk material. The shear stress at the punch surface can reach the saturation value predicted for the bulk material. This insight is critical for understanding friction-induced microstructural evolution in plastically deformable systems. It also underscores the need for advanced modeling approaches—particularly those based on the “third body” concept—that can account for the coupled evolution of deformation and BL formation.
